papers.title: A novel behavioral paradigm for characterizing anticipatory postural adjustments in mice
papers.abstract: Voluntary movements perturb the body's equilibrium, and the nervous system limits this disturbance by generating anticipatory postural adjustments (APAs) that redistribute body weight before and during movement. APAs have been characterized extensively in humans and larger animal models, but the absence of a tractable behavioral assay in mice has limited access to the genetic and circuit-level tools needed to investigate their neural basis. Here, we describe a force-plate behavioral paradigm in which freely moving mice stand on four independent load cells, receive an auditory GO cue and initiate locomotion voluntarily without task-specific training. Using force recordings, high-speed video and markerless pose estimation, we show that mice initiate a step with a stereotyped sequence of weight shifts: the center of pressure (CoP) moves anteriorly and then laterally away from the swing side, the swing forepaw and diagonally opposite hindpaw unload, and body weight is carried by the remaining diagonal pair. A single principal component explained approximately 80% of the variance in the average trial, compared with approximately 50% when paw identity was shuffled. Pressure recordings identified rapid swing-forepaw unloading beginning, on average, 87.9 ms before lift-off. Head and ear movement began approximately 200 ms before lift-off, and an operational multimodal estimate placed the interval between the earliest detected postural movement and the onset of forepaw rotation at approximately 160-180 ms. Neuropixels recordings from the pontine reticular nucleus (PRN) and supplementary motor area (SMA), monosynaptic tracing of inputs to reticulospinal PRN neurons, and preliminary cell-ablation experiments identify the PRN as a candidate node in the circuitry supporting anticipatory postural control. This paradigm provides a platform for circuit-level investigation of postural control and its disruption in disease.

papers.title: Hyperglycemia-responsive circRNA drives diabetic neuropathic pain by competing for PUM2 binding and promoting proNT3/CCL2 in DRG neurons
papers.abstract: Diabetic neuropathic pain (DNP), one of the most common and debilitating complications of diabetes mellitus (DM), remains poorly managed by conventional analgesics, highlighting the urgent need to explore its etiology-associated mechanisms. Here, we identified a novel conserved circular RNA, cRps6kb1, that is significantly upregulated in dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons across multiple mouse models of type 1 DM and type 2 DM, as well as in human donors with DNP. Blocking cRps6kb1 upregulation attenuated the increases in DRG neurotrophin-3 mRNA (Nt3), its encoded proneurotrophin-3 (proNT3), and downstream C-C chemokine ligand 2 (CCL2) expression, as well as the persistence of nociceptive hypersensitivity under the conditions of streptozotocin-induced type 1 DM or high-fat diet-fed type 2 DM. Conversely, mimicking cRps6kb1 upregulation increased DRG Nt3, proNT3, and CCL2 levels and produced DNP-like symptoms in naive mice. In addition, high glucose increased the expression of cRps6kb1 and Nt3 in cultured DRG neurons from mice and human donors. Mechanistically, upregulated cRps6kb1 competed with the Nt3 3'-untranslated region (3-UTR) for the translational repressor PUM2 binding, releasing PUM2 from the Nt3 3-UTR and enhancing Nt3 mRNA translation and stability. Thus, cRps6kb1 is a key contributor to DNP and represents a promising therapeutic target for its treatment.

papers.title: Tri-Modal Single-Cell Atlas of Developing Human Brain
papers.abstract: Epigenetic modifications, such as DNA methylation, evolve throughout development and aging, providing remarkable regulatory diversity and contributing to disease etiology, including neuropsychiatric disorders. However, how these regulatory layers interact across human brain development remains unclear. Leveraging ME-seq, we simultaneously mapped gene expression, chromatin accessibility, and DNA methylation in over 340,000 single nuclei from 40 human brain specimens spanning fetal development to adolescence. Chromatin accessibility and DNA methylation captured partially overlapping cis-regulatory associations. Developmental trajectories revealed distinct temporal kinetics: DNA methylation continued remodeling beyond major transcriptional and accessibility transitions, while developmental clocks yielded modality-dependent age estimates. Modality-specific regulatory networks converged on developmental transcription factors, whereas methylation-defined regulatory regions provided complementary annotations of neuropsychiatric genetic risk. Together, these findings establish DNA methylation as a persistent and complementary dimension of developmental regulation, linking prolonged remodeling to human brain maturation and disease susceptibility.

papers.title: Learned associations constrain anticipatory visual dynamics and enhance sensory and motor readiness to facilitate perceptual decisions
papers.abstract: Learned cue target associations can guide attention to facilitate perceptual decision making, yet how they shape the content and dynamics of neural activity, and whether this facilitation reflects anticipatory preparation, post-target sensory enhancement, or both, remains unclear. Here, we used magnetoencephalography while participants made living/nonliving judgments about visual objects (e.g., cat/violin) with left- or right-hand button presses. Cue category associations were established through repeated pairings: predictive cues always preceded one target category, whereas uninformative cues preceded both categories equally often. Predictive cues facilitated behavioral responses despite limited explicit awareness of the learned associations. Representational similarity analysis showed that prediction preactivated target-specific representations in the visual cortex resembling target evoked activity before target onset. Prediction also elicited anticipatory, response specific motor beta suppression. Together, these findings supported anticipatory preparation, with little evidence of enhanced posttarget visual specificity. Posttarget visual specificity and anticipatory motor preparation independently predicted response speed, with hierarchical drift diffusion modeling linking greater visual specificity to faster evidence accumulation and stronger motor preparation to shorter nondecision time (a model parameter reflecting sensory encoding and motor execution). Beyond representational content, prediction also constrained the evolution of anticipatory visual population activity, and more constrained, stable early visual trajectories predicted faster responses. These population dynamics were associated with faster evidence accumulation, lower decision thresholds, and shorter non-decision time. Together, these findings suggest that associative memory facilitates perceptual decisions by shaping the content and dynamics of anticipatory neural activity, with partially dissociable contributions from visual processing and motor preparation.

papers.title: Advanced meditation stabilizes cortical dynamics through inhibitory gain control linked to absorptive depth
papers.abstract: Advanced meditation can shift conscious experience from ordinary body- and world-centered awareness toward absorption, detachment and dissociation-like states, yet the neural mechanisms that stabilize these immersive states remain unclear. We studied 18 long-term meditators during eyes-open rest and Rajyoga meditation, a practice in which practitioners reduce bodily identification while enhancing inner self-awareness. We combined multidimensional neural approach including frontal EEG spectral power, temporal non-stationarity and corticothalamic neural-field modeling, because these measures probe underlying complementary levels of the brain state transition: the strength of neural activity, its temporal stability, and the circuit level inhibition-excitation gain mechanisms. This framework is especially relevant to meditation because oscillatory, temporal organization may distinguish stable meditative states, and corticothalamic dynamics are closely linked to arousal and conscious state regulation. We correlated meditation induced neural changes with subjective ratings of absorption and dissociation. Compared with rest, meditation was associated with higher beta1, beta2 and gamma power, with no change in the slower bands (delta, theta and alpha), and with lower beta-band temporal non-stationarity, indicating a more stable expression of fast cortical dynamics. Fitting the corticothalamic model to the EEG spectra showed stronger cortical inhibitory gain and lower effective intracortical gain, placing meditation in an inhibition-dominant regime, with lower gain in the loop between excitatory and inhibitory neurons within the cortex. During meditation, these model estimates were related to subjective absorption and showed trend level links with dissociation. Together, these findings suggest that Rajyoga meditation stabilizes cortical dynamics through inhibitory gain control, linking absorption (deep and steady attention on the meditation) to dissociation-like self-detachment.

papers.title: Striatal dopamine availability peaks in adulthood and undergoes age-dependent modulation
papers.abstract: Age is a risk factor for several psychiatric disorders. An adolescent peak in striatal dopamine availability is thought to contribute to the neuropsychiatric vulnerability. However, the lifespan trajectory of striatal dopamine release capacity is undefined in most species. Here, we measured lifespan trajectories of striatal dopamine in primates and rodents and identified a delayed developmental peak in adulthood and age-dependent changes in dopamine release regulation by GABA and acetylcholine across species.

papers.title: Distinct input-output relationships between basal forebrain subnuclei underlie heterogeneous cholinergic modulation of the mouse cortex
papers.abstract: The basal forebrain (BF) supports many behavioral functions via its brain-wide projections, which can be recruited independently and task specifically. However, the anatomical underpinnings for this functional heterogeneity are poorly understood. Here, we compared two mouse BF subnuclei, the horizontal diagonal band (HDB) and the substantial innominata (SI), in terms of their anatomical connectivity and functional recruitment. Using anterograde and retrograde tracing, we show that they target largely segregated forebrain regions, but their input comes from a partially overlapping subset of regions. However, many neurons within each region project to just one of the subnuclei, suggesting they can be recruited independently. To test this, we combined optogenetics and widefield Ca2+ imaging and showed that stimulating prefrontal cortical projections to the HDB or SI results in distinct large-scale patterns of cortical activity via a cholinergic mechanism. Our results provide an anatomical basis for the flexible, area-specific cholinergic modulation of brain function.

papers.title: Neuropathological assessment of cerebrovascular integrity in Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy
papers.abstract: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy neuropathological change (CTE-NC) is defined by perivascular deposits of phosphorylated tau, with lesions preferentially located at sulcal depths. We investigated whether CTE-NC is associated with structural changes to perivascular spaces (PVSs) or microvascular degeneration. Post-mortem middle frontal gyrus tissue from 11 CTE-NC cases and 11 age-matched controls was examined using immunohistochemistry. All CTE-NC cases exhibited pathognomonic lesions in this region. We quantified PVS width along with vessel lumen and PVS area, string vessel burden, pericyte density, and aquaporin-4 (AQP4) polarisation to the astrocytic endfoot. Total PVS width did not differ significantly between the groups in grey matter (P = 0.543) nor white matter (P = 0.468). Neither PVS area (sulcal depth, P = 0.097; gyral crest, P = 0.645) nor PVS-to-lumen area ratio (sulcal depth, P = 0.454; gyral crest, P = 0.307) differed significantly. Similarly, there were no significant differences in total microvascular length (p = 0.693), string vessel burden (p = 0.128), pericyte density (p = 0.589), or AQP4 endfoot enrichment (p = 0.538). We therefore found no evidence of large-scale PVS enlargement, lumen narrowing, capillary degeneration, pericyte loss, or altered AQP4 endfoot enrichment in CTE-NC at the locations and spatial scales investigated. Taken together, these findings suggest that the pathognomonic perivascular tau lesion is not associated with a classical small vessel degenerative phenotype in CTE-NC. However, that does not exclude more subtle molecular, functional, or ultrastructural changes at the interface between vessels, the perivascular space, and surrounding brain tissue.

papers.title: A common neural axis links image distinctiveness and memorability
papers.abstract: Stimulus-specific memorability, the tendency for people to remember and forget the same stimuli, is a powerful predictor of memory performance that is independent of the study and retrieval factors that have dominated memory research. Critically, memorability can be defined in two ways: "Hit-ability" (H-ability) and "false alarm-ability" (FA-ability), the probability of correctly recognizing studied items or falsely recognizing unstudied items, respectively. Although past work has suggested that these are dissociable facets of memorability, challenging single-factor explanations, we present neural and computational evidence that they share a common neural axis. The neural signature of high H-ability matched the signature for low FA-ability, showing that these parameters have inverse relationships with a common factor. Moreover, we show that image distinctiveness predicts the flipped relationship between H-ability and FA-ability in both behavior and neural activity, providing a unifying explanation of stimulus-specific memorability.

papers.title: Transcriptional and DNA Methylation Changes in the Hippocampus and Prefrontal Cortex after Fractionated Cranial Radiation in Mice
papers.abstract: Fractionated whole-brain irradiation is essential for treating brain tumors, but many long-term survivors develop cognitive decline whose molecular basis is poorly understood. We asked which cell types and gene programs change late after irradiation, how the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex compare, and whether DNA methylation changes affect the same genes or programs. Male and female mice received whole-brain irradiation (5 x 4 Gy) or anesthesia alone. Irradiated mice showed persistent deficits in executive function and spatial memory. Eleven weeks after irradiation, single-nucleus RNA sequencing and whole-genome bisulfite sequencing of pooled hippocampal (CA1-3) and prefrontal tissue showed cell-type-specific transcriptional changes in neurons of both regions. Both regions showed reduced ribosomal-protein gene expression and changes in adhesion genes, with reduced respiratory-chain genes in prefrontal neurons and bidirectional synaptic gene changes in hippocampus. Differentially methylated regions were enriched at promoters, with hypermethylation predominating in three of the four sex-by-region contrasts. Methylation and gene expression changes pointed to overlapping synaptic and signaling programs, largely through different genes.

papers.title: A protocol for cortical and deep-brain calcium imaging in freely moving mice with the Mini2P system.
papers.abstract: Two-photon calcium imaging has transformed our understanding of neuronal circuit function, yet conventional approaches require head fixation, limiting the study of neural activity during natural behavior. Miniaturized two-photon microscopy (Mini2P) overcomes this constraint by enabling calcium imaging in freely moving animals while preserving the optical single-cell resolution of conventional two-photon microscopy. However, its implementation requires the careful integration of multiple technically demanding procedures, presenting substantial challenges for laboratories adopting this approach. Here, we present a comprehensive, step-by-step protocol for implementing Mini2P calcium imaging in freely moving mice, emphasizing procedures that are unique to or particularly critical for successful implementation of this technique. This protocol covers system preparation and performance checks, optical alignment, field-of-view selection, baseplate installation, and strategies for maintaining imaging stability during microscope attachment and reattachment. We also address behavioral habituation, integration with behavioral tasks, imaging acquisition, quality control, and troubleshooting as a part of an integrated experimental workflow. Representative imaging data acquired through cranial windows in the primary visual and somatosensory cortices, and through a gradient-index lens in the medial prefrontal cortex, illustrate the applicability of this workflow across different brain regions and optical preparations. Designed for adaptation across brain regions and behavioral paradigms, the protocol provides practical guidance for identifying technical challenges and verifying successful implementation. By establishing clear decision points, validation criteria, and troubleshooting strategies at each stage, this workflow aims to improve reproducibility and facilitate the adoption of the Mini2P for investigating neuronal circuit dynamics during freely moving behavior.

papers.title: Maternal E-Cigarette Exposure Exacerbates Neonatal Ischemic Brain Injury Through the miR-30c-5p-Neurod1 Axis
papers.abstract: Background: Neonatal ischemic stroke is an important cause of mortality and long-term neurological morbidity in infants. Maternal smoking and e-cigarette exposure are recognized risk factors for adverse neonatal outcomes, but the mechanisms underlying increased susceptibility to ischemic brain injury remain unclear. This study investigated whether dysregulation of the miR-30c-5p-Neurod1 axis contributes to this susceptibility. Methods: Pregnant rats were exposed to e-cigarette aerosols from embryonic day 4 to 20. Studies were conducted in male offspring on postnatal day 10. Baseline molecular changes were assessed using microRNA sequencing, quantitative reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction, Western blotting, RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC) and luciferase reporter assays. Ischemic injury was evaluated following transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO). Flow cytometry and molecular analyses were performed to characterize associated cellular changes. The effects of in vivo miR-30c-5p mimic administration, Neurod1 knockdown, and miR-30c-5p inhibition were also investigated. Results: Maternal e-cigarette exposure increased tMCAO-induced infarct size and was associated with increased apoptosis and senescence-associated changes, together with reduced expression of markers of neurogenesis and synaptic development. Under baseline conditions, microRNA profiling and molecular analyses revealed increased miR-30c-5p expression and decreased Neurod1 mRNA and protein levels in the neonatal brain. RISC and luciferase reporter assays supported an interaction between miR-30c-5p and Neurod1 mRNA. In vivo administration of a miR-30c-5p mimic reduced Neurod1 expression and increased infarct size, whereas Neurod1 knockdown independently exacerbated ischemic injury and associated cellular changes. Conversely, inhibition of miR-30c-5p restored Neurod1 expression, reduced infarct size, and ameliorated associated pathological changes. Conclusions: Maternal e-cigarette exposure is associated with baseline dysregulation of the miR-30c-5p-Neurod1 axis and increased susceptibility to neonatal ischemic brain injury in male rats. These findings suggest that this regulatory axis may contribute to the effects of prenatal e-cigarette exposure on the developing brain and may increase susceptibility to neonatal ischemic stroke.

papers.title: Exploring subacute effects of a DMT and harmine meditation retreat on the brain's control energy landscape
papers.abstract: Modeling the brain as a controllable structural network allows the estimation of the control energy (CE) required to reach functional states, where low-CE states are more accessible. Psychedelics are thought to acutely flatten the brain's CE landscape, broadening the repertoire of reachable states, but whether this reorganization persists into the subacute ``afterglow" window is largely unknown. This exploratory study uses rs-fMRI from a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (N = 39; 19 verum [N,N-dimethyltryptamine (DMT) + harmine, Ayahuasca-inspired formulation], 20 placebo) scanned before and after a three-day meditation retreat. We compute CE on a group human connectome project (HCP) structural connectome under two approaches that emphasize long and short timescale dynamics. Globally, we found no systematic shift in the distribution of CE between transitions, however mean CE increased in both groups at the long timescale approach. Surviving network effects emerge when a network's intrinsic timescale matches the stabilization regime. In the long timescale regime, the central executive network (CEN) showed an increase in post-retreat CE within the verum group that survived Benjamini-Hochberg False Discovery Rate (FDR-BH) correction. Although CE and functional connectivity are distinct, this higher CEN cost may relate to the reduced within-network connectivity previously reported subacutely after psilocybin. The default mode network (DMN) also showed a post-retreat CE increase in both groups, but neither change survived FDR correction. In the short timescale approach, the visual network (VN) showed a FDR-BH CE decrease within the verum group, consistent with reduced dynamical demand in a region acutely engaged by DMT. To examine whether changes were concentrated in less accessible states, we additionally analyzed rare brain states, defined by the top decile of information content. This analysis revealed a modest session x condition interaction in the long timescale approach. Overall, the two timescale lenses surface different network effects, that align with cortical timescale hierarchies. These findings point to network- and timescale-specific, rather than global, CE changes in the afterglow window, though effects are small and heterogeneous and require confirmation in larger samples. Characterizing whether and where psychedelic effects persist into the subacute window is relevant to psychedelic-assisted therapy, including safety, therapeutic timing, and durability of drug effects. More broadly, considering cortical timescale hierarchies may help identify network-specific CE changes that might be less apparent when networks are evaluated under a single dynamical timescale.

papers.title: Local goodness-of-fit measures for neural decoding
papers.abstract: State-space models are widely used to relate neural activity to internal states that cannot be observed directly, but assessing whether a given model is appropriate for a dataset remains difficult. Current approaches, such as cross-validation, summarize model fit across an entire recording. They can reveal that a model is imperfect, but not when during the recording it fits poorly. We therefore lack tools for targeted model refinement. Here, we develop local goodness-of-fit measures that ask whether each spike is consistent with the model's prediction based on all preceding spikes. Each spike, through the tuning of the neuron that fired, points to a range of likely states, just as the prediction does. A spike that narrows a broad prediction is consistent with it; one that points to states the prediction considers unlikely is not. Because the comparison needs only the prediction and the states each spike points to, it also applies to models that decode from unsorted spike waveforms. Using simulations in which model errors are known, we show that two consistency measures, based on the overlap of high-probability regions and on predictive checks, flag such inconsistent spikes, whereas the standard Kullback-Leibler divergence also flags spikes that merely narrow a broad prediction. We then apply the measures to a hippocampal recording from a rat performing a spatial foraging task. In these data, a model assuming continuous movement is expected to fail during immobility, when the hippocampal representation can jump to distant locations, so we compare it with a model that also allows such jumps. As expected, the overlap measure flags more spikes during immobility than during movement under the continuous model, and allowing jumps removes most of the continuous model's flags. The consistency measures thus show when during a recording a state-space model fits poorly, providing tools for its targeted refinement.

papers.title: Sleep deprivation differentially recruits amygdala subregions in male and female mice
papers.abstract: Sleep deprivation (SD) acutely increases negative affect, and chronic insufficient sleep is associated with an increased risk of depression. Since the amygdala regulates both emotional processing and sleep, and SD dysregulates amygdalar function, amygdala functionality may link sleep loss to emotional outcomes. To better understand this, the specific sleep-impacted amygdalar nuclei need to be fully defined. To determine the impact of acute sleep loss on the relative activation of specific amygdalar regions, we screened for the neuronal activity marker c-Fos in wildtype mice that slept undisturbed, underwent 4-h SD, or 4-h SD with 2-h recovery sleep (RS). Application of whole-brain clearing and automated cell counting identified increased c-Fos expression within the cortical subplate of both male and female mice that was localized to amygdalar regions. As the amygdala comprises multiple distinct subnuclei, we parcellated and quantified c-Fos expression within each amygdalar subnucleus. Interestingly, we found that SD-induced differential c-Fos expression patterns between sexes. In male mice, SD increased c-Fos expression across several amygdalar subnuclei, which largely reversed with RS. By contrast, SD in females increased c-Fos expression only in the anterior basolateral amygdala and the intercalated amygdala, and both subnuclei remained activated even with RS. These findings highlight sex-specific spatial distribution of SD-activated amygdala cells, which may contribute to differences in emotional processing following sleep loss and offer potential anatomical targets for mitigating SD-related mood deficits.

papers.title: Differential effects of AMPA receptor inhibition on seizure-like events in murine and human brain slices
papers.abstract: Epilepsy is a frequent neurological condition with a worldwide prevalence of 0.5-1%. Current therapies are limited by adverse effects as well as drug resistance. This highlights the need for novel, target-specific antiseizure medications with improved efficacy and fewer side effects. AMPA (-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid) receptors represent a therapeutic target as demonstrated by perampanel, an AMPA receptor antagonist used clinically as antiseizure medication. AMPA receptors typically mediate fast excitatory neurotransmission. Their properties are modulated by auxiliary proteins that can alter receptor activation, deactivation and desensitization, including converting them into slow AMPA receptors. In this study, we tested different AMPA receptor inhibitors, including perampanel, for their ability to suppress seizure-like events (SLE). SLE were recorded with extracellular electrodes in cortical brain slices from healthy mice and from epilepsy patients who underwent resective surgery. SLE were induced with 4-aminopyridine (4-AP) or a combination of 4-AP and high-potassium. We found that seizure-like events in murine tissue appeared more frequently, with higher amplitude and spike frequency, but were briefer than in human tissue. GYKI53655, NBQX and perampanel were equally effective in inhibiting SLE in murine und human brain slices. In contrast, the antagonist LY3130481, specific for the AMPA receptor auxiliary protein {gamma}-8, showed only weak efficacy in murine tissue, but blocked of SLE in human tissue almost completely. The species-specific differences we found for LY3130481 highlight the benefit of using human tissue in preclinical research and underline that auxiliary subunits remain a promising therapeutic target for the development of new antiseizure medications.

papers.title: High spatiotemporal resolution in vivo imaging reveals preferential PACAP38 action on dural vasculature and a functional therapeutic readout
papers.abstract: PACAP38-induced cephalic vasodilation is used to assess functional PACAP pathway inhibition in humans, but the vascular populations underlying this response are not fully resolved. Defining these compartments in a preclinical model could help connect clinical pharmacodynamic responses with the underlying vascular mechanisms and support further development of PACAP-targeted therapies. Using chronic cranial windows and head-mounted microscopy, we tracked meningeal vascular responses in freely moving mice. Nitroglycerin, levcromakalim, and PACAP38 each produced net vasodilation, yet the underlying responses were markedly heterogeneous and distributed differently across the vascular populations. Notably, PACAP38 evoked greater early vasodilation in dural than pial vessels, and anti-PACAP pretreatment attenuated PACAP38-induced vasodilation. These findings show that net vasodilation can conceal vessel-level response patterns and identify preferential early dural vasodilation as a spatially defined, pharmacologically modifiable feature of the systemic PACAP38 response. This phenotype provides a translational platform for mechanistic interrogation and evaluation of functional pathway inhibition by migraine-targeted therapies.

papers.title: Sensory context gates oxytocin effects on auditory processing in macaques
papers.abstract: Oxytocin shapes social perception, yet its neural effects vary substantially across experiments and clinical trials yield inconsistent results. A key unresolved question is whether oxytocin modulates early sensory processing in primates as a function of sensory context. Using high-resolution pharmacological fMRI in two awake rhesus macaques, we compared systemic oxytocin with saline during unimodal auditory and audiovisual tasks. During unimodal auditory stimulation, oxytocin attenuated sound-evoked responses throughout auditory core, belt and associative regions for both vocal and non-vocal sounds, while distributed sound-category information remained decodable. In contrast, when the same vocalizations were presented within an audiovisual task, this attenuation disappeared and responses increased in a restricted set of auditory core and belt regions. Oxytocin also reorganized resting-state coupling among auditory, visual and prefrontal systems and changed how evoked responses covaried across runs. Together, these findings suggest that oxytocin modulates sensory response magnitude and inter-regional coordination in a context-dependent manner rather than uniformly enhancing social signals.

papers.title: AKAP-CaN-NFATc3 signaling drives persistent inhibitory long-term potentiation
papers.abstract: GABAergic inhibitory synaptic plasticity has critical roles in neuronal function, synaptic plasticity, and cognition. Activity-dependent alterations in gene expression are essential for generating long-term changes in inhibitory postsynaptic strength, yet the signaling mechanisms that drive inhibitory postsynaptic plasticity are not well understood. During an important form of inhibitory long-term potentiation (iLTP), NMDA receptor (NMDAR) activity promotes de novo synthesis of GABAA receptors (GABAARs) and the inhibitory scaffold, gephyrin, leading to persistent strengthening of inhibition. However, it remains unclear what activity-dependent signaling mechanisms control these changes in gene expression to maintain iLTP. In this study, we identify that activation of the transcription factor, nuclear-factor of activated T-cells (NFAT), and anchoring of the phosphatase, calcineurin (CaN), to A-kinase anchoring protein (AKAP79/150) are crucial in regulating long-term structural and functional GABAergic postsynaptic plasticity. Using short hairpin RNA (shRNA) to knock-down hippocampal NFAT isoform, NFATc3, we demonstrate its requirement for the synthesis of new inhibitory synaptic proteins, inhibitory synapse growth, and strengthening of synaptic currents during persistent iLTP. Additionally, using a knock-in mouse line containing a mutation in the CaN binding region of AKAP, we find that AKAP-CaN signaling lies upstream of NFATc3 activation and is required for increased inhibitory synapse clustering and synapse strengthening during iLTP via regulation of miRNA transcriptional activity and protein synthesis. Thus, we have identified an excitation-transcription coupling pathway that rapidly controls the synthesis of new inhibitory synaptic proteins and maintains persistent inhibitory synaptic plasticity, an essential process for memory formation and cognition in the brain.

papers.title: A Glutamate-Neuropeptide Circuit Converts Transient Mate Contact into a Persistent Local Search State in Caenorhabditis elegans Males
papers.abstract: Transient sensory encounters can trigger behavioral states that persist long after the initiating stimulus has disappeared, yet how neural circuits initiate and sustain these states remains poorly understood. Here, we show that brief contact with a suitable mate induces a persistent local search state in male Caenorhabditis elegans, characterized by increased reversals and spatially restricted exploration that continues after mate removal. Transient optogenetic activation of male-specific ray type B (RnB) sensory neurons recapitulates this state, with its magnitude and persistence increasing with stimulation strength. Glutamatergic signaling promotes neuronal responses within the interconnected RnB sensory network and contributes to prolonged activity in downstream LUA interneurons. In contrast, loss of the LUA-derived neuropeptide NLP-13 or its receptor DMSR-2 preserves initial stimulus-evoked neuronal responses but reduces prolonged LUA calcium activity and behavioral persistence. LUA-specific restoration of NLP-13 rescues persistent local search, identifying these interneurons as a functionally important source of the neuropeptide. Together, our findings reveal complementary contributions of glutamatergic and neuropeptidergic signaling to the generation and persistence of behavioral states, illustrating how distinct signaling mechanisms cooperate to transform transient social encounters into prolonged circuit activity and persistent behavior.

papers.title: A Complete Three-Dimensional Spiral Ganglion Neuron Map in a Human Adult using a Deep Learning Pipeline
papers.abstract: The quantity and distribution of spiral ganglion neurons (SGNs) greatly influence speech and hearing ability. Historically, approaches to quantify SGNs from archival human temporal bones (TBs) have utilized only every 10th section to estimate the total SGN count. The current study evaluates a novel deep-learning pipeline for SGN quantification to produce the first complete three-dimensional SGN map of the human cochlea using every tissue section. The reconstruction is based on one adult human cochlea in which all 421 consecutive, 20 um thick, celloidin-embedded sections were H&E stained, mounted and digitized. SGN nuclei were manually labeled in training sections which were subsequently used to create UNet++ models for SGN detection. These models were then applied to all other sections and compared to manual counts by three experienced histopathologists. After quantification, serial sections were aligned and SGNs were assigned percent distances along Rosenthal's canal and characteristic frequencies using a modified Greenwood formula. Models to automatically identify SGN nuclei from digitized tissue sections performed with great accuracy: SGNs were counted in 191 sections with 97% accuracy compared to manual counts. When tissue sections were systematically omitted, counting only every 10th section was determined sufficient to ensure a median inferred total count accuracy of 98%. We present a new, flexible machine learning pipeline for identifying SGNs in digitized human TBs. Further, we show the first full 3D visualization of all 27,880 SGNs in an adult human cochlea, with associated tonotopic maps and basal-to-apical SGN distributions.

papers.title: Interpreting computational mechanism from multi-area neural recordings
papers.abstract: Distilling computational mechanisms from neural recordings requires disambiguating intrinsic dynamics from external inputs. Here, we introduce Dynamically Interacting Systems (DynISys), a multi-compartment dynamical-systems model that infers per-area dynamics and structured inter-area communication from multi-area spiking activity. DynISys combines neural ordinary differential equation (ODE) latent dynamics with injective latent-to-neural mappings to achieve expressive and trustworthy dynamical inference. When applied to simultaneous dorsal premotor (PMd) and primary motor (M1) recordings from a continuous reaching task, DynISys accurately reconstructs neuronal responses without inventing spurious latent features. Analyzing the model's dynamics reveals putative mechanisms for motor planning and execution, with PMd-to-M1 inputs positioning a stable fixed point in M1 that encodes execution dynamics for the upcoming movement, subsequently evoked by external (non-PMd) inputs. Finally, multi-session DynISys achieves consistent latents when fit to neural recordings spanning multiple days. In summary, DynISys allows distillation of multi-area recordings into an interpretable account of distributed neural computation.

papers.title: Aperiodic Exponent as an EEG Marker of Interoceptive Attention during Gastric Fullness
papers.abstract: Gastric interoceptive attention to internal, bodily signals such as hunger, satiety, and fullness are important for regulating feeding behaviors. However, abnormal processing or sensitivity to these can lead to disorders that result in overly restrictive or excessive consumption, highlighting the need for better understanding of the cortical processing of these cues. Specifically, understanding cortical representations of self-perceived gastric fullness have yet to be studied in humans. In this work, we demonstrate that consistently across individuals, the broadband power spectral density of EEG signals, as quantified by the aperiodic exponent, flattens after individuals drink water until fullness. Simultaneous measures of the stomach and heart demonstrate increased vagal drive to peripheral organs. We further find that changes in cortical aperiodic exponent patterns are associated with changes in the frequency of gastric oscillations. Overall, this suggests that the EEG aperiodic exponent may be a useful noninvasive biomarker for assessing gastric interoceptive attention.

papers.title: Synaptotagmin 7 differentially regulates synaptic vesicle trafficking at tonic and phasic synapses
papers.abstract: Synaptic vesicle (SV) release probability can differ across neuronal subtypes, but the molecular mechanisms establishing such differences remain incompletely understood. In the current study we demonstrate that Synaptotagmin 7 (SYT7), a calcium-sensor regulating SV trafficking, is enriched at Drosophila tonic Ib synapses compared with phasic Is synapses. Loss of SYT7 preferentially enhanced evoked release at Ib terminals, whereas overexpression strongly suppressed fusion at both neuronal subtypes. High-frequency stimulation partially overcomes this inhibition, producing robust facilitation. Ultrastructural analysis revealed that SYT7 overexpression preserved morphologically docked SVs while promoting accumulation of enlarged presynaptic cisternae and redistribution of SV-associated proteins. Conversely, SYT7 loss reduced activity-induced presynaptic cisternae, suggesting an important role in regulating the bulk endocytosis pathway. Together, these findings identify differential SYT7 abundance as a contributor to tonic and phasic synaptic diversity and reveal a role for SYT7 in coordinating SV release and presynaptic membrane cycling.

papers.title: INSULIN MODULATES FOOD VALENCE THROUGH ASTROCYTES
papers.abstract: Brain cells involved in assigning affective value (i.e.: valence) to stimuli modulating brain states are not yet fully identified. Since astrocytes modulate brain states, and insulin regulates feeding behavior and exerts its central actions in part through astrocytes, we analyzed the role of the insulin receptor in astrocytes in assigning valence to food. We used the modulatory actions of food on anxiety and fear, as proxies of the affective influence of food on mood. Mice lacking insulin receptors (IR) in GFAP astrocytes (GFAP-IR KO mice) showed increased anxiety and fear in response to food, while control littermates showed the opposite behavior. Since orexin neurons in the lateral hypothalamus (LH) are involved in fear conditioning, and are inhibited by feeding, we determined whether they are involved in mood alterations observed in fear-conditioned fed GFAP-IR KO mice. We observed increased c-fos expression in orexin neurons of these animals, indicating that the lack of IR in astrocytes modifies the response of these neurons to food. Moreover, chemogenetic stimulation of LH astrocytes in fed GFAP-IR KO mice was sufficient to significantly attenuate their fear responses. These findings suggest that astrocytic insulin receptors modulate the responses of hypothalamic orexin neurons to food. We speculate that cellular mechanisms underlying eating disorders may involve insulin modulation of food valence through astrocytes.

papers.title: Chronic FMNL2 overexpression is associated with changes in brain histology and exploratory behavior in adult zebrafish
papers.abstract: Formin-like protein 2 (FMNL2) has been associated with Alzheimer`s disease and cerebrovascular pathology and regulates gliovascular remodeling following amyloid exposure. However, the consequences of sustained FMNL2 elevation remain unclear. We generated a transgenic zebrafish line expressing human FMNL2 under the her4.1 promoter and examined adult brain histology and behavior under baseline conditions and following acute amyloid-{beta}42 (A{beta}42) exposure. Histological analyses assessed FMNL2 immunoreactivity, overlap between the glial marker BLBP and endothelial tight-junction marker ZO1, synaptic vesicle protein SV2 labeling, and microglial counts. Exploratory behavior was evaluated using the novel tank test and free-movement pattern Y-maze. Compared with uninjected wild-type controls, uninjected FMNL2-overexpressing fish showed higher FMNL2 immunoreactivity, lower BLBP-ZO1 overlap, fewer normalized SV2 puncta, and higher counts of total and morphologically activated microglia. Acute A{beta}42 exposure in wild-type animals produced changes in the same direction across these histological endpoints. No significant additional histological changes were detected following A{beta}42 exposure in the overexpression background. In the novel tank test, uninjected FMNL2-overexpressing fish had a higher composite boldness index than uninjected wild-type controls. These findings indicate that sustained FMNL2 overexpression is associated with histological changes resembling several responses to acute A{beta}42 exposure, together with altered exploratory behavior. They support further investigation of persistent FMNL2 elevation as a contributor to altered glial-vascular organization and cellular responses relevant to Alzheimer`s disease.

papers.title: CoReg, tracking-based motion compensation for in vivo calcium imaging
papers.abstract: In vivo calcium imaging enables the observation of neural activity with high spatial and temporal resolution. However, recordings are frequently affected by motion artifacts caused by animal movement, physiological processes, tissue drift, or instability of the imaging setup. These artifacts make signal extraction harder and reduce the consistency of downstream analyses. Current registration methods can correct rigid and non-rigid motion, but often estimate motion from individual frames or image patches and make limited use of temporal information. In addition, activity-driven fluorescence changes can make it difficult to distinguish changes in image appearance from actual motion. Here, we treat motion correction in calcium imaging as a point tracking problem and introduce CoReg, an open-source Python- based software tool with a graphical user interface. We benchmark CoReg against established registration methods using fluorescence imaging datasets from multiple species. CoReg performs competitively with or better than existing approaches across several settings. We further show that its performance is robust to the choice of tracked points, making the method straightforward to apply. CoReg includes implementations of both our method and the evaluated established methods. Our results show that tracking-based registration provides a simple and reliable approach for motion correction in vivo calcium imaging.

papers.title: A shared slowing axis and phenotype-specific rhythms link clinical EEG to FDG-PET dementia phenotypes
papers.abstract: Early and accurate identification of neurodegenerative disorders has notable implications for treatment and quality of life. Whereas neuroimaging-based biomarkers can accurately identify neurodegenerative subtypes, EEG represents a low-cost alternative that could expand access to dementia care. Here, we investigated whether six data-driven EEG latent factors, derived by nonnegative tensor decomposition of clinical EEGs, differ systematically across FDG-PET-defined neurodegenerative phenotypes. In 455 patients with EEG and FDG-PET acquired within one year of each other, factor expression was compared across 14 diagnostic classes assigned by StateViewer, a validated artificial intelligence framework for FDG-PET interpretation. To separate disease-general severity from phenotype-specific topography, each factor was also regressed on a subject-level slowing index. Finally, we related the factors to regional FDG uptake and to neuropsychological performance (n = 98) and assessed their potential utility for single-subject classification. Four factors reflecting neurophysiological oscillations (posterior alpha, Rolandic beta, frontotemporal delta-theta and posterior theta-slow alpha) varied significantly across phenotypes, with attenuation of faster and augmentation of slower rhythms most pronounced in dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), dysexecutive Alzheimer disease (AD) and posterior cortical atrophy, whereas factors dominated by eye-movement and muscle artifact showed no robust phenotypic association. Alpha and beta effects were largely attributable to overall slowing, whereas posterior theta-slow alpha became more phenotype-specific after adjustment (eta-squared 0.082 to 0.147), dissociating the Alzheimer disease spectrum from frontotemporal syndromes. The slowing index tracked with an FDG-PET pattern highly associated with DLB across the cohort, irrespective of assigned phenotype (r = 0.51, P 0.8) but poorly discriminated frontotemporal dementia phenotypes canonically associated with 4-repeat tau. Thus, data-driven decomposition of clinical EEG separates oscillatory activity from artifact into factors that track metabolic phenotype, regional metabolism and cognition, capturing both overall slowing and phenotype-specific patterns. This work informs the further development of scalable, biology-informed EEG-based phenotyping of neurodegenerative disease.

papers.title: A modified Arrestin1 Slows Retinal Degeneration Across Genetically Distinct Mouse Models of Inherited Retinal Disease
papers.abstract: Inherited retinal diseases (IRDs) are a genetically heterogeneous group of disorders caused by mutations in more than 340 genes, limiting the applicability of gene-targeted therapies and creating the need for broader treatment strategies. Photoreceptor dysfunction is a hallmark of IRDs and often results in disrupted retinal metabolic homeostasis, as photoreceptors have exceptionally high metabolic demands and provide metabolic resources to surrounding retinal cells. Consequently, enhancing retinal metabolism has emerged as a promising gene-agnostic strategy for treating IRDs. We previously developed a modified arrestin1 (ArrGG) that relieves arrestin1-mediated inhibition of the glycolytic enzyme enolase1, thereby increasing glycolytic output and slowing retinal degeneration in the RhoP23H/+ mouse model. Here, we investigated the therapeutic potential of ArrGG as a gene-agnostic approach targeting endogenous metabolic enzyme activity across genetically distinct models of IRD. Using two complementary photoreceptor-enriched transcriptomic analyses, we found no widespread, reproducible transcriptional changes following ArrGG treatment. These findings support our hypothesis that ArrGG modulates photoreceptor metabolism without inducing substantial transcriptional remodeling. The therapeutic efficacy of ArrGG was evaluated in three IRD mouse models representing rapid rod degeneration (rd10), cone degeneration (GC1KO), and RPE-associated retinal degeneration (rd6). ArrGG treatment was associated with preserved retinal function and slowed structural degeneration across all three models. Together, these findings support the potential of modulating endogenous metabolic enzyme activity to preserve photoreceptors across genetically distinct IRD models. This work suggests that ArrGG could be a promising gene-agnostic metabolic therapy for slowing retinal degeneration and preserving visual function in inherited retinal diseases.

papers.title: Evidence of silent nociceptor activation during the formalin test in rats
papers.abstract: Background: Abnormal ongoing activity in C-mechano-insensitive (C-Mi) nociceptors is seen in patients with chronic pain. These 'silent' nociceptors are often under-reported in preclinical pain models - precisely because they aren't mechanically sensitive. The formalin test is widely used as a preclinical model of persistent sensitisation characterised by two behavioural phases, where phase 2 is considered to reflect central sensitisation and the role of peripheral afferent drive in its maintenance is disputed. Increased activity in C-mechanosensitive (C-M) nociceptors has been reported during both phases, but the behaviour of C-Mi nociceptors has not been assessed. Methods: Multi-contact microneurography was conducted from the saphenous nerve of male and female rats. An activity dependent slowing protocol was used to segregate C-fibres, and responses to mechanical stimuli were assessed. Formalin- (2.5%) or saline-evoked activity was then assessed during the two test phases. Results: 168 A- and C-fibres were identified with latency tracking, and classified using activity dependent slowing into C-M and C-Mi nociceptors. ADS-classified C-Mi nociceptors were active in both phase 1 and phase 2 (33.3% and 31.0%, n=18 and n=16, respectively). We find no evidence that formalin mechanically sensitises C-Mi nociceptors or alters the ADS profiles of C-fibres. There was no sex specific difference in C-fibre classes or the effect of formalin. Conclusions: These results indicate the presence of ongoing activity in a substantial population of C-Mi nociceptors in a commonly used persistent pain assay that may play a role in the sensitisation that is seen in phase 2 of the behavioural response.
